target_audience: University students or advanced high school students studying Linear Algebra

sections.title: The Mystery of the Treasure Map
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a linear system using a narrative. Imagine a robot named 'Vector-Bot' trying to find a treasure at coordinates (x, y). The treasure is defined by two intersecting paths (linear equations). We define the system as Ax = b, where A is the transformation matrix and b is the target vector.
sections.example: Vector-Bot is given two instructions: 2x + 1y = 4 and 1x + 2y = 5. We want to find the exact values of x and y that satisfy both.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Determinant as Area
sections.content: Before solving, we must visualize the determinant. In 2D, the determinant of a matrix represents the signed area of the parallelogram formed by its column vectors (v1 and v2). This area represents the 'scaling factor' of the transformation.
sections.example: Animate two vectors v1=(2,1) and v2=(1,2). Show the parallelogram they form on a grid. Calculate the area (det = 3) and highlight it with a semi-transparent color.

sections.title: The Geometric Setup of Ax = b
sections.content: Explain that the equation Ax = b means we are stretching vector v1 by a factor of 'x' and vector v2 by a factor of 'y' to reach the target vector 'b'. The goal of Cramer's rule is to find these specific stretching factors.
sections.example: Show vector 'b' (4,5) as the result of a linear combination: x units along the transformed v1 axis and y units along the transformed v2 axis.

sections.title: The 'Shear' Insight for x
sections.content: To find 'x', we create a new parallelogram using 'b' and 'v2'. Because b = x*v1 + y*v2, the area of the parallelogram (b, v2) is equal to the area of (x*v1 + y*v2, v2). Since adding a multiple of a vector to another (shearing) doesn't change the area, this simplifies to the area of (x*v1, v2), which is just x times the original area (v1, v2).
sections.example: Animate the parallelogram (v1, v2) shifting its first side to 'b'. Show visually that the 'y*v2' component doesn't add any area because it's parallel to the base v2.

sections.title: Deriving the Ratio (Cramer's Formula)
sections.content: If Area(b, v2) = x * Area(v1, v2), then x must be the ratio of these two areas. This is the heart of Cramer's Rule: x = det(Ab)/det(A), where Ab is the matrix formed by replacing the first column with the target vector b.
sections.example: Display the math: x = Area(target_parallelogram) / Area(basis_parallelogram). Show the numbers: x = det([4, 1; 5, 2]) / det([2, 1; 1, 2]) = 3 / 3 = 1.

sections.title: Scaling to y and Summary
sections.content: Briefly demonstrate that the same logic applies to 'y' by replacing the second column with 'b'. Conclude by emphasizing that Cramer's Rule is simply comparing how much 'area' the target vector contributes relative to the original basis vectors.
sections.example: Final visual recap: Vector-Bot reaches the treasure at (1, 2) by calculating the ratios of areas. Show the final formula neatly on screen: xi = det(Ai) / det(A).
